Age is a significant factor when looking at roles.� A child s role responsibility gradually increases with age until a person finally reaches adult status. Slowly the status of an adult may decline as old age approaches and the elderly may lose power and prestige in the society.

Transitions between role categories are not smooth or well defined.� For example, many teenagers complain that they are treated like children sometimes and expected to act as adult other times.


Traditional cultures help their people transition from role to role by having distinct age/responsibility designations.� �A major difference is that the elderly are made treated as intellectuals and have a definite place in decision-making matters. Modern conveniences blur the lines of these designations.� For example, a seventeen year old has driving privileges but probably still lives at home with their parents.� An elderly person may exercise, eat well and has the benefit of modern medicines and cosmetics.� This means that a sixty-five year old grandmother may look and feel more like a forty year old woman.

A very interesting example of modern medicine confusing age roles is the fact that some women, with help from doctors, are giving to birth to children while being fifty to sixty years old.
